title: How Cleft Lips and Palates Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain cleft lip and cleft palate, covering what they are (a visual birth defect, not a disability), how they form in the embryo, types (incomplete, complete, submucosal cleft palate), risk factors (genetics, smoking and drinking during pregnancy, folic acid, diabetes, obesity, some epilepsy medications), prevalence by ethnicity, feeding challenges, ear infections and speech issues, treatment timeline (cheiloplasty, palatoplasty, nasoalveolar molding, bone grafts, rhinoplasty, jaw surgery), parental bonding and overprotectiveness, global disparities and charities Smile Train and Operation Smile, famous people with clefts, and adoption of children with clefts. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about the slang "Netflix and Chill."

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to clefts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the word literally, a baseball game, and Chuck's return to in-person recording. They introduce cleft as a division or void, define cleft lip and palate as a common birth defect and visual difference rather than a disability, and say the term hair lip should not be used.

segments.title: Embryonic formation of the lip and palate
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the upper lip, nose, and palate form from separate tissue plates early in pregnancy, around weeks four to seven, and that a cleft occurs when these do not fuse. They describe the philtrum, the hard and soft palate, and the difference between incomplete and complete clefts. Cleft lip is always of the upper lip.

segments.title: Causes, risk factors, and prevalence
segments.summary: Genetics, a parent or sibling with a cleft, and genetic syndromes raise risk. Smoking, drinking, diabetes, obesity, and some epilepsy medications are risk factors. Folic acid supplementation is discussed. Causes are multifactorial. Prevalence is higher among Native Americans and Asian people and lowest among African Americans. Submucosal cleft palate is noted as often hidden.

segments.title: Health challenges and feeding
segments.summary: Clefts can affect tooth development, which may require bone grafts, and can cause feeding difficulty with latching and suction. A cleft lip is easier to feed around, while a cleft palate needs specialized bottles. Breast milk is less irritating than formula if it gets into the nose and ears. Children with clefts have more ear infections, sometimes hearing and speech issues.

segments.title: Surgical treatment timeline
segments.summary: Diagnosis often happens by ultrasound for cleft lip and after birth for cleft palate. Lip repair (cheiloplasty) can occur as early as three months and before one year. Palate repair (palatoplasty) comes later, before eighteen months. Nasoalveolar molding, a retainer-like device, can reduce follow-up surgeries. Later procedures include speech therapy, rhinoplasty, and jaw alignment surgery.

segments.title: Parents, bonding, and cost
segments.summary: The hosts discuss parents' worries about bonding after a diagnosis, research finding no bonding differences, the risk of overprotectiveness, teasing, and the scarring from surgery. They mention out-of-pocket costs of around two hundred thousand dollars average over a lifetime, with uncertainty about whether insurance is counted.

segments.title: Global challenges and charities
segments.summary: In developing countries, stigma is worse and blame often falls on mothers; a Kenya study reported mothers contemplating harm. Access to care is harder. Smile Train and Operation Smile train local doctors instead of only sending in surgeons. Operation Smile runs thirty-one medical centers in sixteen countries.

segments.title: Famous people with clefts and adoption
segments.summary: The hosts list famous people with clefts or cleft scars, including Stacy Keach, Joaquin Phoenix, Peyton Manning, and Cheech Marin, and mention Wendy Williams's comment about Phoenix. They describe adopting children with unrepaired clefts and the Rainbow Kids agency that connects adoptive parents with children with special needs.

segments.title: Listener mail: Netflix and Chill
segments.summary: Chuck admits he did not know the slang Netflix and Chill, which a listener named Rosie said means having sex. The hosts laugh about it and invite listener email.
